speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with both confidence and pleasure that I rise for the first time to make

my maiden speech in this house. I say "with confidence", because although I am making my maiden speech I am in the position of being a frontbencher. The only misgiving I feel is of course that the only way I can go from here is backwards. I should like, first of all, to extend congratulations to you on your election to your present office, and congratulate also the Deputy Speaker and the hon. members who moved and seconded the address.
I should also mention at this time that in addition to finding myself a frontbencher during this debate I was also treated to another surprise. You may recall, sir, that immediately after the speech from the throne during the reception you held I had the pleasure of being introduced to you as a senator. I have smiled at the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) continuously, and studied my notes and letters assiduously, but I wish to assure you that, fortunately or unfortunately, my status has not changed as yet.
I should like to refer for a moment to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who beat a somewhat hasty retreat from some of his remarks when the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) intervened. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is I believe a historian, is experiencing a difficulty which at present confronts a good many hon. members-he is living in the past. He attributed the victory of the Conservative party to a saturation of advertising. I suggest that instead of saturation with advertising it was satiation with Liberalism which was the cause of the great Conservative victory.
I feel, perhaps, that it is almost unfair to make any reference to the group sitting on your left owing to the smallness of its numbers, but I cannot refrain from doing so. I think the reduction in their numbers is, perhaps, a form of penalty derived from the fact that they were on a mythical train shuttling between Regina and Winnipeg, from one manifesto to another; and during the shuttling back and forth there was no time for some of them to get aboard. I say this with discrimination, because I see in his place the silvery-voiced bard from Kootenay West who may have some interjection to make at this point. If there is no interjection, I wish to turn for a moment to the riding of Burnaby-Richmond which I have the pleasure to represent.
As other speakers have done before me, I should like to give a brief description of my riding. The area of Burnaby is in British Columbia, bounded on the north by Burrard inlet, on the south by the Fraser river, on the west by a suburb known as Vancouver city,
The Address-Mr. Drysdale and on the east by another suburb known as New Westminster. The riding of Richmond, which is another municipality, is at the mouth of the Fraser river, while further west are a series of islands-Lulu island which is an extremely large island, Sea island and other smaller islands.
I should like to borrow the House of Commons for the time being and rearrange it verbally; I assure hon. members that none of the furniture will be moved. I would, by way of illustration, suggest that the treasury benches, as being perhaps the highest point in the house, should represent the municipality of Burnaby. I would then take this broad green sward as representative of the Fraser river; the colour is not true, it is much more like the grey of the walls, the swirling, muddy Fraser. I would place Lulu island at the Clerk's desk, and where the reporter is sitting-I hope he does not get his feet wet- I would place Sea island, one of the largest airports in the country. From that airport one can fly in 15 minutes to Victoria, or in 15 hours to Amsterdam. I think it is appropriate that the golden mace should be on Lulu island because we have there the golden developments of the future, the embodiment of the spirit of the golden west.
Incidentally, the municipality of Burnaby is some 40 square miles in area, and that of Richmond approximately 58 square miles. We have had a great deal of housing development in those areas.
4 I should like to turn now to the speech from the throne and make a few suggestions to the various occupants of the treasury benches. I hope these suggestions will be taken as made as matters to be considered rather than as criticism of the government. In the first place, I should like to extend the appreciation of my constituents as far as the housing program is concerned, and of the authorization of $350 million for this purpose, a large portion of which will, I hope, go to both Burnaby and Richmond, such funds being badly needed by the construction industry in that area. The momentary curtailment of money available for housing a few weeks ago struck a serious blow to the construction industry. In addition, I should like to extend my appreciation to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for extending seasonal benefits to the unemployed. This should help to remedy an immediate problem which the two municipalities are facing.
Turning to another of the matters mentioned in the speech from the throne, it is reported in connection with airports that there will be a large expansion of the system of airports and airways. I should like at this point to raise a very important problem. As I mentioned, Vancouver airport is one of the

The Address-Mr. Drysdale largest airports in Canada and one of the busiest. The airport is used by light plane operators, but due to the increasing traffic among the numerous airlines it has become necessary to move the light plane operators. The suggested location is Port Moody about 18 air miles from Vancouver airport. This location, which has been protested to me by light plane owners and operators, is perhaps one of the worst possible locations from the standpoints of fog and accessibility, and I should like to suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) that they consider the establishment of the airport at Boundary bay.
At present, Boundary bay airport, which is extremely close to Vancouver and easy of access, is occupied by a wireless station controlled by the Department of National Defence, and I would ask the minister to consider the possibility of moving the wireless station. An objection has been expressed by the Department of Transport that due to the closeness of Vancouver airport this airport at Boundary bay would impinge on the flight path of the airliners. I would point out to the minister that at the Boeing field in Seattle where light planes are taking off we have the Seattle-Tacoma airport where there is heavy airplane service and it is only a distance of seven miles away. Apparently in that situation the flight-ways are not interfered with.
I would like to turn for a moment to the question of harbours and rivers. I notice in the speech from the throne there is a prediction of increased work. I would like to direct to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) the interest of the municipality of Burnaby in seeing that, in the dredging of the Fraser river, the spoilage which comes up from the Fraser be placed on some 1,100 acres which the municipality is extremely anxious to reclaim. In order to have an adequate reclamation scheme the fill must be placed on this land to a depth of some three feet which, of course, is a considerable amount to be dredged but it would assist the municipality a great deal.
While dealing with the Fraser river I would like to consider the needs of the municipality of Richmond. In this connection we require -I think it is imperative so far as time is concerned-an assembly dock. At present the sea traffic goes up the southern arm to New Westminster. While I feel that New Westminster is an extremely adequate port, with the expansion of the golden west it is necessary that we have an assembly dock at the earliest possible moment.
Let me turn to the prediction in the speech from the throne of the establishment of a railway to the Great Slave lake area. I would

like to take a broader view of British Columbia and urge on the government that when this railway is established it be so established that we can have a connection with the Pacific Great Eastern. The Pacific Great Eastern railway goes south to Vancouver, the gateway to the Pacific. Since this government has predicted an increase in trade I feel that this is one of the better ways to increase trade.
Another matter that was mentioned in the speech from the throne was fisheries. It was stated in the speech from the throne that the government would continue its unremitting efforts to sell fish. I must point out that in this year, which is the centennial year in British Columbia, the festivities are even being joined in by the sockeye salmon. In 1954 there was a run of some 12 million salmon, of which 9i million were caught. It is predicted that this year, the centennial year, the run will exceed that of 1954.
While on the matter of fish I should like to discuss very briefly an extremely contentious issue which is very important to the people of my constituency, especially in the town of Steveston, because they are dependent entirely on the fishing industry. I refer to the question of fish versus power. I would urge on the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) that he consider at the earliest possible moment the implementation of what might almost be described as a crash program in doing research into the fishing industry, with a view to providing means of getting the salmon upstream past dams and again downstream and safely out to sea. At. present that problem has not been solved, and the proximity of the Fraser to the Vancouver area makes it perhaps the front line for the fish and power development problem. Although we realize the necessity of power development, the fishing industry has been one of the great industries of Canada for many years. It has been the backbone of one of the basic industries of Canada. I would like to see a continuation of the fishing industry. In order to do that it is imperative that we have proper research.
I am extremely pleased to see the establishment of a small business section within the administrative machinery of government. This is of particular interest to the people of my riding because of the number of small businesses in my constituency. I am also pleased to know that there will be amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act. In connection with the citizenship act and matters of immigration, I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) the problem of a group of Japanese Canadians within my area. Prior to leaving for Ottawa

I was approached by a group who set forth to me the problems affecting this particular group. As you are aware, shortly after the war Japanese Canadians were deprived of their British nationality and their Canadian citizenship. At the present time perhaps 100 Japanese in my area are affected, people who have gone to Japan because they had no place to go and who have been deprived of their nationality and citizenship. A fairly large number of these people are desirous of returning to Canada. I would appreciate on behalf of those people any consideration that could be given to facilitating their return to Canada.
Another problem with the Japanese Canadians is that approximately 50 of the women residing in this particular area who are Japanese-born and came to Canada and have lived here for perhaps 20 years are in the position of being unable to get Canadian citizenship owing to the fact that they are unable to speak English. Under the present Canadian Citizenship Act, I believe it is section 10, subsection 1(e), there is the provision that English be spoken or, in the alternative, if the person has lived here for more than 20 years Canadian citizenship may be granted. I would urge the minister to send a directive to the county court judges in the Vancouver area drawing to their attention the provisions of this particular section.
Another problem of the Japanese Canadians is the difficulty of immigration. I do not refer to the general problem of immigration but to the problem of the sons and daughters who are resident in Canada and whose parents are resident in Japan. Under the present limits it is necessary that the mother be over 65 years of age and the father over 70 years of age. I would urge the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to consider the possibility of either reducing or eliminating the age limit entirely.
I return very briefly to a general discussion of the problems of municipal finance. As you are aware, the municipalities are faced with the difficulty that land is perhaps the major source of revenue. As you will realize, it is one of the most inflexible tax bases we have. I draw it briefly to the attention of the government and urge that they consider, first, federal aid to education to alleviate this tremendous burden being placed on the municipalities. Second, I would suggest that a revolving fund be established from which the municipalities could borrow money to construct badly needed capital projects at very low interest rates. I would further urge, that consideration be given to exempting the municipalities from the 10 per cent federal tax on such items as 57071-3-22
The Address-Mr. Dumas machinery, sewer pipe, and so forth, being used by the municipalities exclusively.
At this time, as a new member, I would like to commend what has been the very excellent and perhaps sympathetic attention at times by the various civil servants in the various departments of government. I would say, not as a member of parliament, that I have approached many of these departments purely as an individual coming in off the street and I have been impressed continuously with their sincerity and also the extremely quick service I have received.
I might add that I am extremely pleased to see that the messengers now have their own uniforms. The lack of them caused considerable confusion so far as I was concerned because I was having difficulty distinguishing the messengers from hon. members. This resulted in one embarrassing situation. I rang for a messenger and through sheer coincidence a minister of our provincial government appeared in the doorway. I started to send him on the message but fortunately realized the situation.
As I have already mentioned, this is centennial year in British Columbia. Since at the present time we have a fair amount of available space both in Richmond and Burnaby I should like to suggest that if consideration is going to be given to having parliament sit during the summer months it might be moved to the west coast. I realize the difficulties but I have endured Ottawa weather for the past three weeks embracing everything from snow to rain and high humidity. I feel it would be a tremendous advantage and help our spirits to have parliament on the west coast.
As we enter the parliament buildings we see the motto over the doorway with the words "from sea to sea, both east and west". I think that the Conservative party embodies that motto extremely well because we have unity from coast to coast, representation from every province and representation in both languages.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should be grateful if you would convey to the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) my most sincere congratulations on his re-election to the highly important position of first commoner.
To you personally, I offer my warmest congratulations on your appointment to the post of Deputy Speaker. It is a great and well-deserved honour.
I am happy to associate myself with all previous speakers in congratulating the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. La-freniere) for the manner in which he carried
330	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dumas out the difficult and very honourable task of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
(Text):
I am also very happy to offer my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) for his contribution as seconder of the address. His knowledge of the north will be an asset not only to his party but also to all of us who are keenly interested in the problems of northern Canada.
I intend, Mr. Speaker, to confine most of my remarks to one sector of our economy, namely the mining industry. However, before I elaborate on this subject I hope I will be permitted to comment on some of the proposals outlined in the speech from the throne. In the speech from the throne we are told that we will be asked to approve a number of measures and appropriations in order to sustain employment by the acceleration of useful public works and by encouraging the development and processing of our natural resources. We are also made aware that we will be asked to make provision for a substantial program of public investment to be carried out by government departments and crown companies and to provide assistance to provincial governments for certain agreed types of projects. Particular mention is made of airport facilities and airway systems, harbours and rivers and public buildings.
In order to promote national development in the north we are also told that we will be asked to authorize the construction of a railway line to Great Slave lake and to pi'ovide for the construction of important roads needed for development in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and in the provinces, this with the co-operation of their governments. The government also proposes the initiation of a program of research to assist the opening up of the mineral resources of the Arctic islands.
The speech from the throne contains many other proposals including two which have already been disposed of, the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and the National Housing Act. The impression is created that most of the proposals outlined in the speech from the throne are new and bold proposals when in fact few of them are in these categories. This so-called antirecession program as detailed in the speech from the throne is not too clear by any means. If we exclude the increased public funds to be made available under the National Housing Act, certainly nothing has been suggested specifically that would put men to work tomorrow. By the time the house has disposed of some of these proposals and by the time some of them come out of the survey stage we will have to deal with


another winter season and we will have to face another wave of seasonal unemployment.
In the field of public works, for instance, it would seem to me that the government could have been much more aggressive. The government, in consultation with the provinces and with their co-operation, should have taken the necessary steps by this time in order to make available to Canadian municipalities at reasonable rates of interest much needed funds so as to enable them to carry on a large program of municipal improvements. A measure of this kind could have been presented to parliament in the early stage of the session and work could have been started immediately. This would have had an immediate effect in boosting employment and on a much larger scale than would any projects that could be undertaken directly by the federal government.
Although the total value of Canadian mineral production during 1957 exceeded that of 1956 by $50 million, some sectors of the industry experienced very serious difficulties during that same period. The three traditional base metals, copper, lead and zinc, are still having plenty of troubles and unless we find some way of correcting the situation we will have a much larger decline in the production of these three base metals during 1958. The general softening of world markets during the last 12 months was generally reflected in the mining industry. Demand for most of the mineral products slackened and diminished and, of course, prices dropped.
This trend was much more accentuated for copper, lead and zinc. For instance, the price of copper which was at an all-time high early in 1956, fell by more than 40 per cent in the latter part of 1957. The prices for lead and zinc also dropped by approximately 20 per cent and 25 per cent respectively during the same period. Shipments of copper, lead and zinc during 1957 declined by $93 million; $6 million and $26 million respectively.
In Canada these adverse conditions in the production of copper, lead and zinc had some serious repercussions. Several mines had to suspend or close their operations, while others had to cut back production. The outlook for the immediate future of the mining industry is not too good. The three major base metals, copper, lead and zinc, are experiencing some serious trouble. Copper stocks in the United States are at their highest level in 19 years. However, there is a possibility that the price of copper may be heading upward again. Canadian and United States prices have been fairly steady for the last few weeks.
The same thing cannot be said about lead and zinc. The price of lead sank another half-cent in New York last week. It was reduced to 11J cents a pound, which is the lowest level since July, 1950. The cut was the second

in 1958 and brought the total decline during the last 12 months to 4J cents. The latest statistics for the zinc industry in the United States confirm the continued unsatisfactory position of this metal. There is just too much of both lead and zinc. According to a recent survey made by the Northern Miner we find that in the first four months of 1958 not only are producers having their problems but the possibilities of further cutbacks are anticipated unless there is a pickup in demand during the coming months.
The production of iron ore and of asbestos is going to be much below last year's level unless the demand picks up strongly in the second half of 1958. Besides these problems of oversupply, reduced consumption and low prices which I have just mentioned, the Canadian producers of copper, lead and zinc may suffer additional setbacks if the administration in the United States is shortsighted enough to give way to those who are promoting higher tariffs for these commodities. The threat of increased duties on Canadian lead and zinc entering the United States is a very serious one. Until we are assured that this threat is not to become a reality the Canadian government should not cease its efforts to avoid the imposition of these duties, because once they are imposed there is a danger that they may remain permanently.
The Canadian copper producers are alarmed also by the proposal currently before the United States congress aimed at reimposing the import duty on copper which has been suspended since April, 1951. Unless the powers of the President of the United States to control trade and tariffs are extended a tax of 1.7 to 2 cents a pound on copper goes into effect automatically on July 1 next. It is to be hoped that the administration will succeed in having these presidential powers extended.
On May 14 last I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) concerning this matter, as recorded at page 64 of Hansard for that date. I particularly asked:
-what steps have been taken to implement the recommendations made to him recently by the Canadian Metal Mining Association regarding the possible reimposition of import duties on Canadian copper by the United States?
The minister's answer, in short, was that the views of the Canadian government as to the importance of ensuring that there is no increase in tariffs or other barriers to the export of base metals from Canada to the United States have been made known to the United States government. Well, this is not enough. As I said previously, there should be no easing whatsoever of the effort of the Canadian government in these matters until 57071-3-22J
The Address-Mr. Dumas we are absolutely sure that the threat of increased duties on our three major base metals has completely disappeared. It has been made clear to the minister by the Canadian Metal Mining Association that the effects of such action on the part of the United States upon our Canadian mining industry would be most disastrous to say the least.
It is true that in lieu of granting increased tariffs as recommended by the tariff commission the United States administration has made a proposal whereby there would be a system of price support in the form of subsidies for copper, lead and zinc and other base metals produced in the United States. The first general response in this country to this plan was distinctly favourable. It is believed here that the few cents of subsidy proposed in this plan would maintain the United States mining industry but would not stimulate any great amount of extra production which might reduce sales from other countries.
However, it appears now that this plan is meeting with strong opposition from United States producers and mining circles in the United States. It is said that the plan has no great chance of passing congress. This is most unfortunate because I am sure that such a proposal, in lieu of higher tariffs, would have helped the Canadian mining industry. What is more important, it would have created an atmosphere of goodwill and bonne entente between our two countries. In view of the possibility of this plan failing, it is not surprising to hear that Canadan base metal producers are again warning one another of the necessity of renewing the strong opposition of this country to United States metal tariff proposals.
Having said this, I feel that the government should give very serious consideration to another proposal made by the Canadian Metal Mining Association, under which it would be of the utmost importance that the Canadian government impress on the administration of the United States the crucial importance of Canada's metals, minerals and energy resources for the continued strength of the United States' domestic economy and the common interests of our joint defence. Moreover, as pointed out by the Canadian Metal Mining Association, it is of vital importance that the attention of the United States government be constantly and pointedly drawn to the fact that their growing dependence on this country for strategic metals, fuels and energy sources is completely inconsistent with their policy of trade restriction. A comprehensive plan for the systematic development of Canada's resources and their best use in the interests of economic growth and joint defence is highly desirable.

The Address-Mr. Dumas
Similar steps have been taken in the past and I do not see why they cannot be taken again. I express the hope that the proposal outlined by the Canadian Metal Mining Association will be given high priority.
If at the present time the situation of the Canadian mining industry is not what we should like it to be, nevertheless we have every reason to be optimistic and to believe that the long range outlook is as promising as it can be.
In recent years the industry has played an outstanding role in Canadian economic development. At present it is a vital sector of our economy and its future is almost unlimited. In order to substantiate this statement I should like to quote just two or three paragraphs of the final report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. At page 211, commenting on the increased production since 1930, the report states as follows:
Moreover, the stimulus this increased production has given to investment outlays both directly and indirectly through its requirements for new power, transport, manufacturing, housing and social capital facilities has been one of the main dynamics of our growth throughout the post-war period. Indeed, despite the increasing diversity and maturity of the Canadian economy, the high level of demand for our valuable mineral and other resources has been one of the principal reasons why the rate of our national expansion has outpaced that of most of the other economies of the free world since 1945.
Further, at page 229, in the concluding remarks of the report we read this:
In summary, the anticipated growth and development of our mining and mineral processing industry is expected to raise the industry to a position in the Canadian economy in which it will surpass the forest industries and will fall not very far short of agriculture in its contribution to over-all domestic output.
Then in the last paragraph of this "Conclusion" we read as follows:
The further substantial growth which is foreseen for the mining and mineral processing industry suggests that in every respect it can be safely regarded as a soundly-based and strong contributor to the Canadian economy.
Canada is bound to obtain an increasing share of an expanding world demand for metals and minerals and the Canadian producers can look forward with confidence to long-term markets. In the meantime, however, everything must be done to keep the industry as healthy as possible. We must do everything we can to keep employment in the mines at as high a level as possible. We must make sure that the Canadian producers are not forced into high-grading their ores and thus reducing the life of their mines. We must encourage prospecting and exploration by all means possible. We have the know-how, we have a well and fully manned department of mines, and there are no reasons

for this country to stand still in this domain. At times we may have to take some extraordinary measures. If this has to be done, we should not hesitate. This is one sector of the economy which we should keep healthy and strong.
In the speech from the throne we find that during the course of this session amendments will be proposed to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. In this regard I should like to make a few suggestions to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois).
First, if the government is of the opinion that other matters should have priority during the early part of the session, and consequently if the amendments to E.G.M.A. are to be dealt with only in the latter part of the session, I would suggest to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys that he make an announcement at the earliest possible time and tell the house the nature of the amendments. An early announcement in this regard would be of great advantage. It would permit the industry to plan more effectively for the future. Moreover, if these proposed amendments are such that they constitute an entirely new approach to the problem-and I hope they are of this nature-and may create strong enough incentive so as to stimulate prospecting, exploration and development and thus encourage more employment in the mining industry, I would say that now is the time to come forward with such an announcement.
Second, if the government has not already decided on the exact form these amendments will take, or if it has not finalized these amendments, I would suggest that careful and serious consideration should be given to the recommendations presented, in the form of a well elaborated brief, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys some two weeks ago by a group of Canadian gold mining communities. One practical approach to the problem has been suggested by the Canadian gold mining communities in their brief and I should like to bring it to the attention of the house. At the same time I will remind the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys of the good approach proposed in this brief. At page 88 of the brief we find the following:
A Combination Policy for Gold-Another possible policy would involve retaining the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in substantially its present form, but with certain important amendments.
First, the word "emergency"-
This is not very important, however.
-and the concept of the emergency could be dropped from the letter and the spirit of the act. The purpose: to get the statute onto a normal, long-term footing.

Second, the act could be amended to give mines another option with respect to it. At present a mine may elect to be eligible for cost aid or to sell its gold in the open market during certain periods of the year. A third choice could be ofTered: to sell gold to the Royal Canadian Mint at some statutory price higher than $35 an ounce.
Such a combination policy-a combination of higher price and continued cost aid-need not be more costly to the public treasury. It would reflect, in part, an extension of the spirit of assistance to marginal mines and communities which the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act originally embodied.
There is no question, that a firmer basis for gold mining operations would do much more than assist the managements and employees of the mines. It would put at least some producers in a more profitable position, with resulting tax benefits to provincial and federal gov ernments. It would do more than relieve the uncertainty now gripping the gold mining communities. A better deal for gold would have economic effects far beyond the immediate horizons of those persons who work or live near the mines.
I sincerely hope that the proposed amendments to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act will be such that they will give a new life to the industry and that they will be most beneficial to the mines and to others living in the gold mining communities. At this time a strong and effective approach to this problem would have positive economic implications far beyond the mines and related communities; on exploration and development of base metals, for instance, on Canada's foreign trade position and on manufacturing throughout the country.
Another step which should be taken by the government at this time is the introduction of a measure to ease the situation for some of the base metal mines by amending the regulations granting a three year tax exemption to a new mine, in a way which would make it possible for a mine to elect to defer its tax exemption for 1958 and to carry it over to the end of the normal 36 months' period. This question was brought to the attention of the government by the Canadian Metal Mining Association and in proposing such an amendment the association submitted the following argument. With your permission, Mr. Speaker,
I would like to quote from page 7 of the association's report, which is entitled "The Mining Industry in Canada 1957", as follows: Some dozen mining companies, operating within the first three years of commercial production, find themselves in the position of having to decide whether or not to close operations as a result of the fall in base metal prices. It is felt that such an amendment as proposed would Induce such companies to remain in operation and to retain the services of their employees at a time of seriously mounting unemployment throughout Canada.
The Address-Mr. Dorion
Further on in the detailed report the Canadian Metal Mining Association has this to say regarding the legislation which was passed many years ago:
The three-year tax-exemption granted to new mines has been a most valuable piece of legislation. Certainly, as a result of it, a number of mining companies have come into operation in Canada which otherwise might never have developed at all. This provision is one that is highly prized by the industry. All regard it as a highly effective piece of incentive legislation.
I believe the end of my time is approaching and in conclusion I would like to emphasize again that we must always be on the alert as far as the Canadian mining industry is concerned. This industry must not be permitted to deteriorate. In pleading the case of the mining industry I am not only trying to promote the betterment of this very important sector of our economy; I am fighting for the very survival of the principal industry in my own constituency of Villeneuve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not without a vivid and intense emotion that a newcomer rises to deliver his maiden speech in this house. How could it be otherwise when we stand before representatives who come from the four corners of our country, each with his own ideas and feelings and each different, one from the other.
There are also the senior members who for many years have acquired experience in politics, in administration and in parliamentary law and whose standard of knowledge and competence appear to us so inaccessible. There is moreover, all around the memories of those famous men who, each in his turn, have appeared in this house and have participated in the great task of ensuring to our country the enviable place it presently holds in the concert of nations.
The newcomer, regardless of age or experience in other walks of life, feels the need to look around him to discover everything that can help him combat the vigour and intensity of his emotions. Fortunately such help exists, and I have in mind first of all the good nature, the friendliness and the broadmindedness which characterize you, Mr. Speaker, and of which you gave so much outstanding evidence during your career as a public figure.
There exists, furthermore, that spirit of comradeship which springs among all who are engaged in the performance of the same mission-to serve our country to its best of our own ability.
Lastly, there is for the members of the Conservative party the active and dynamic presence of a leader whose sweeping victory of March 31 last bears eloquent witness to the fact that his doctrine and program meet

The Address-Mr. Dorion with the sentiments, the ideas and the highest aspirations of the Canadian nation as a whole.
The province of Quebec chose to contribute liberally to that unprecedented result. If two-thirds of its representation is on the side of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and if it concurred so decisively in his victory, it is not, as was insinuated, because we succeeded in deceiving the electorate of our province or in degrading its conscience. It is positively and entirely because Quebec saw in the leader of our party a statesman equal to those who have best understood our country and its problems and who have endeavoured to give to our confederation- born of agreement between the constituent provinces-the fulfilment of its true purpose and who have respected the liberties of all the participants.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy indeed to associate myself with the expressions of confidence given those who are at this time entrusted with new responsibilities.
It is fitting that mention be made, first of all, of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration <Mrs. Fairclough) whose responsibilities are among the most important and most difficult there are. Her presence in the cabinet is living testimony of our debt to Canadian womanhood. Without Canadian womanhood, without the courage and the devotion which our womenfolk have never ceased to bring to the education and upbringing of our children, our nation could never be strong, vigorous, or conscious of its responsibilities.
I would also like to greet the new Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) who, in spite of his youthfulness, is already a battle-scarred veteran. This is the third time that the electors of the constituency of Labelle have recognized his talents and his worth by electing him to this house. There is no doubt that he will continue to show himself worthy of their confidence in the discharge of the high responsibilities which are now his.
The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) is an old friend of mine. He will no doubt remember certain stirring fights which we had occasion to wage side by side to dispel the prejudice which then attached to our party.
Far from weakening him, unfavourable circumstances seemed to add to his courage. Invariably he fought with that ardour, that conviction, that utter selflessness which finally overcome obstacles and which are the hallmark of great soldiers. He too carried a marshal's baton in his knapsack. The Prime Minister was well advised in inviting h-m


into the council of the nation, and we shall count on him to be the spokesman there of the people of our district.
In becoming vice-chairman of this house the member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) succeeds his illustrious father, who is now one of the leading lights of the Quebec bench. His gallant conduct during the last war, his smiling courage in adversity demonstrate, for all to see, from what strong stock he is sprung. To discharge his duties worthily, he will only have to draw upon paternal tradition, where he will find the impartiality and the sense of justice characteristic of great arbitrators.
The mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Lafreniere and Mr. Nielsen) have been deservedly congratulated, and it is with all my heart that I join in those congratulations. May I remind the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency that I was very happy over his election, all the more so because he is the first Conservative member to represent this constituency since my elder brother took his place in this house in 1930. As I am probably the only one of his electors to sit here and listen to him, I have had the opportunity to appreciate his keen awareness of our local problems and I realized how right we have been to elect him to the house.
Mr. Speaker, it has often been said, as stated in the speeches we have heard so far, that Canada has a great variety of economic areas, each with its own characteristics. This diversification, intensified by the geographic distribution of natural wealth, explains why the economic factors of our country vary so much from one area to the other, from one province to the next. Therefore, to enable the government to build up and introduce legislation designed to extend its good effects over the whole of the country, as far as possible, it is fitting that, at the very beginning of a legislature, the member of parliament should strive to set out the economic conditions of his own constituency. It is with that in mind that I will deal very briefly with two or three of the problems I have at heart and which call for an urgent and effective solution.
In the constituency of Bellechasse there is not one single urban centre. Out of a total population of about 28,000 people, more than 16,000 live on farms. That is why the farm problem must be foremost in the mind of the representative of that area in this house. It also explains to what extent the policy of the Conservative government in that regard was one of the deciding factors of my election.

The Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act has been for my electors a vigorous incentive, especially as the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) was kind enough to invite an agricultural expert from the province of Quebec to become a member of the commission and the general manager of the Cooperative Federee du Quebec, as well as the president of VXJnion Catholique des Cultivateurs to be members of the advisory committee. The government is to be commended for those three appointments. Farmers in these areas will at last have an opportunity to make known their difficulties, to express their point of view and to benefit from the tremendous potential advantages of that legislation.
The constituency of Bellechasse, one of the most picturesque of the Quebec district, is 15 miles downstream from the old capital, on the south shore of the St. Lawrence. It comprises a long strip of land, 50 miles long by about 15 or 20 miles wide, inserted between the constituency of Montmagny on the one side and the constituencies of Levis and Dorchester on the other, even touching the U.S. border southeastward.
It partakes of the three physiographic areas which characterize this whole portion of our district. From north to south, there is first the St. Lawrence plain, generally six to seven miles deep, except for the western part where it extends over a distance of about twelve miles. The altitude varies and may reach up to 500 feet above sea level. The soil is good and all the lands have been occupied for quite a long time.
However, the river waters constantly damage the land and each year wash out thousands of cubic feet of good farming
The Address-Mr. Dorion soil. This erosion is increased by the frequency and intensity of navigation. Former governments dealt with the problem, but so parcimoniously that the work accomplished hardly gave any practical results. A breakwater at St. Vallier and supporting walls all along the coast line, from St. Michel to Berthier inclusively, have now become very necessary.
I trust the Ministers of Transport and Public Works (Mr. Hees and Mr. Green) will join their efforts so that vast projects may be started without delay, and the local unemployed may get some help. The farmers will also benefit from this project, which will allow them to keep the whole of their modest property.
